history.q: Which British navigator charted Australia's east coast in 1770 aboard HMS Endeavour?
history.fact: Cook landed at Kamay Botany Bay in April 1770, where botanist Joseph Banks collected so many new plants that the bay was named for them.

history.q: In which year did the First Fleet arrive at Sydney Cove to found a British penal colony?
history.fact: Eleven ships carrying about 1,500 people, roughly half of them convicts, arrived at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788.

history.q: In which year did the Australian colonies unite to form the Commonwealth of Australia?
history.fact: Federation took effect on 1 January 1901 with a ceremony in Sydney's Centennial Park, uniting six colonies as states.

history.q: Which bushranger wore homemade iron armour in his final shoot-out at Glenrowan in 1880?
history.fact: The armour was hammered from plough parts. Kelly was captured, tried and hanged at the Old Melbourne Gaol that November.

history.q: What does the 'ANZAC' in Anzac Day stand for?
choices: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
Australian Naval and Zealand Air Corps
Army of the New Zealand and Australian Colonies
history.fact: Anzac troops landed at Gallipoli on 25 April 1915; the date is marked every year with dawn services across Australia.

history.q: What discovery set off a population boom in Victoria in the 1850s?
history.fact: Victoria's population rose from about 77,000 in 1851 to over 500,000 a decade later, making Melbourne one of the world's richest cities.

history.q: Roughly how long have Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples lived in Australia?
history.fact: They are often described as the world's oldest continuous living cultures, with hundreds of distinct languages and nations.

history.q: Which former convict settlement on Tasmania's Tasman Peninsula is now a World Heritage site?
history.fact: Founded in 1830 as a timber station, Port Arthur became a prison for repeat offenders sent from across the colonies.

history.q: Which Dutch explorer reached the island now named after him in 1642?
history.fact: Tasman named the island Van Diemen's Land after his patron; it was officially renamed Tasmania in 1856.

history.q: Who commanded the First Fleet and became the first governor of New South Wales?
history.fact: Phillip chose Sydney Cove for its fresh water and deep harbour, naming it after Lord Sydney, the British Home Secretary.

history.q: The 1854 Eureka Stockade was an armed uprising by whom?
history.fact: The miners protested against costly licences; their blue-and-white Southern Cross flag became a lasting symbol of protest.

history.q: Which Australian city was bombed by Japanese aircraft on 19 February 1942?
history.fact: The raid was launched by the same carrier force that attacked Pearl Harbor, and was the first of dozens of raids on Darwin.

history.q: Which explorers led the ill-fated 1860-61 expedition to cross Australia from south to north?
history.fact: They reached the tidal mangroves near the Gulf of Carpentaria but died on the way back; John King survived, cared for by Yandruwandha people.

history.q: Who led the first recorded circumnavigation of Australia in 1801-03 and promoted the name 'Australia'?
history.fact: Flinders sailed with his cat Trim, whose statue now sits on a window ledge of the State Library in Sydney.

history.q: The 1808 Rum Rebellion in Sydney overthrew which governor?
history.fact: Bligh was no stranger to rebellion: in 1789 his crew had seized HMS Bounty in a famous mutiny.

history.q: Roughly how many convicts were transported to Australia between 1788 and 1868?
history.fact: Many Australians today descend from convicts, and having a convict ancestor is now often a point of family pride.

history.q: The 1942 Kokoda Track campaign was fought in which present-day country?
history.fact: Australian troops fought over the steep Owen Stanley Range, helped by Papuan carriers nicknamed the 'Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels'.

history.q: The Immigration Restriction Act, among the first laws of the new federal Parliament in 1901, underpinned which policy?
history.fact: It used a dictation test to exclude migrants; the policy was dismantled in stages and formally ended in 1973.

history.q: Which Dutch captain left an inscribed pewter plate on an island off Western Australia in 1616?
history.fact: Willem de Vlamingh found the plate in 1697 and replaced it with his own; Hartog's plate is now in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

history.q: Who made the first recorded European landing in Australia, on Cape York Peninsula in 1606?
history.fact: Janszoon sailed the small ship Duyfken; later that year Torres passed through the strait that now bears his name.

history.q: Which governor of New South Wales from 1810 to 1821 is often called the 'Father of Australia'?
history.fact: Macquarie built roads, towns and public buildings, many designed by the convict architect Francis Greenway.

history.q: Which colony received Australia's last convict ship, in 1868?
history.fact: The Hougoumont landed at Fremantle; Western Australia had asked for convicts to help build its struggling colony.

history.q: Australian troops nicknamed the 'Rats of Tobruk' held a besieged port in 1941 in which country?
history.fact: The nickname came from enemy propaganda, but the defenders adopted it with pride and held out for months.

history.q: In which city did Aboriginal activists hold a 'Day of Mourning' protest on 26 January 1938?
history.fact: Held on the 150th anniversary of the First Fleet's arrival, it is seen as a landmark of the Aboriginal civil rights movement.

history.q: In 1966 Vincent Lingiari led Gurindji workers in a walk-off from which cattle station?
history.fact: In 1975 Prime Minister Gough Whitlam poured soil into Lingiari's hand as land was handed back to the Gurindji.

technology.q: Which aviation device, now standard on airliners, was invented by Australian scientist David Warren?
choices: The flight data recorder or 'black box'
technology.fact: Warren, whose father died in an air crash in 1934, built his prototype in Melbourne in the 1950s.

technology.q: Which wireless technology was developed with key help from engineers at Australia's CSIRO?
technology.fact: CSIRO's patent on fast wireless networking earned it hundreds of millions of dollars from technology companies.

technology.q: Which curved throwing tool, crafted by Aboriginal peoples for thousands of years, can be made to return to the thrower?
technology.fact: Returning boomerangs were mostly used for sport and hunting birds; heavier non-returning ones were used to hunt larger game.

technology.q: The Hills Hoist, a backyard icon since 1945, is what kind of device?
technology.fact: Lance Hill started making his height-adjustable rotary clothesline in Adelaide, and it soon spread across suburban Australia.

technology.q: Built from 1949 to 1974, the Snowy Mountains Scheme is a vast system of what?
choices: Dams, tunnels and hydroelectric power stations
technology.fact: More than 100,000 people from over 30 countries worked on the scheme, many of them post-war migrants from Europe.

technology.q: In 1988 Australia became the first country to issue banknotes made of what?
technology.fact: Developed with CSIRO to defeat forgers, polymer notes have clear windows and last far longer than paper ones.

technology.q: The Parkes radio telescope in New South Wales helped broadcast TV pictures of which 1969 event?
technology.fact: Parkes and the Honeysuckle Creek station near Canberra relayed the moonwalk images seen by some 600 million people.

technology.q: What nickname do Sydneysiders give the Sydney Harbour Bridge?
technology.fact: Opened in 1932, it has long been listed as the world's widest long-span bridge, and visitors can climb its arch.

technology.q: Western Australia's Pilbara region is famous for mining which mineral, one of Australia's top exports?
technology.fact: Trains in the Pilbara regularly haul ore cars in lines more than 2 km long to ports such as Port Hedland.

technology.q: Australian surgeon Graeme Clark pioneered which medical device?
technology.fact: The first patient received the 'bionic ear' in Melbourne in 1978, and it has since helped hundreds of thousands of people hear.

technology.q: Which train crosses the Nullarbor Plain on the world's longest straight stretch of railway?
technology.fact: The track runs dead straight for 478 km; the train's name reflects its journey between the Indian and Pacific oceans.

technology.q: Ford Australia's Lewis Bandt designed which beloved Australian vehicle type in 1934?
technology.fact: The story goes that a farmer's wife asked for a car to take her to church on Sunday and carry pigs to market on Monday.

technology.q: Which Australian pair won the 2005 Nobel Prize for showing that bacteria cause most stomach ulcers?
technology.fact: To convince sceptics, Marshall drank a culture of Helicobacter pylori and soon developed stomach inflammation.

technology.q: Which Adelaide-born scientist shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for turning penicillin into a usable medicine?
technology.fact: Florey's team in Oxford ran the first trials on patients in 1941; his portrait later appeared on Australia's $50 note.

technology.q: Which Google product grew out of a Sydney start-up co-founded by brothers Lars and Jens Rasmussen?
technology.fact: Google bought their company, Where 2 Technologies, in 2004 and launched Google Maps the following year.

technology.q: Melanie Perkins co-founded which online graphic design platform?
technology.fact: Perkins first ran a school-yearbook design business from her mother's living room in Perth before Canva launched in 2013.

technology.q: The airline name Qantas originally stood for what?
choices: Queensland and Northern Territory Aerial Services
Queensland and New Territories Air Service
Quick Australian National Transport Air Service
Queensland Air Navigation and Transport Association
technology.fact: Founded in 1920 in Winton, Queensland, Qantas is one of the world's oldest continuously operating airlines.

technology.q: In 1928 Charles Kingsford Smith piloted the first flight across which ocean?
technology.fact: His plane, the Southern Cross, flew from California to Brisbane via Hawaii and Fiji; Sydney Airport is named after him.

technology.q: Lawrence Hargrave's experiments in 1890s Sydney produced which aviation invention?
technology.fact: In 1894 Hargrave lifted himself several metres off the ground at Stanwell Park beach using four linked box kites.

technology.q: In the 1850s James Harrison of Geelong pioneered which technology?
technology.fact: Harrison built ice-making machines using vapour compression, and later tried to ship frozen meat to Britain.

technology.q: Australia co-hosts the Square Kilometre Array radio telescope project with which country?
technology.fact: The Australian half, SKA-Low, is being built on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia's Murchison region.

technology.q: Ian Frazer, Australian of the Year in 2006, co-developed a vaccine against which virus?
technology.fact: Frazer and the late Jian Zhou developed the technology behind vaccines that protect against most cervical cancers.

technology.q: Plastic surgeon Fiona Wood co-invented which treatment for burns victims?
technology.fact: Her technique sprays a patient's own skin cells onto wounds; she treated many survivors of the 2002 Bali bombings.

technology.q: Who founded the service that became the Royal Flying Doctor Service, whose first flight was in 1928?
technology.fact: The Presbyterian minister's dream of a 'mantle of safety' for the outback began at Cloncurry; he appears on the $20 note.

technology.q: The mining giant BHP takes its name from which outback town's silver, lead and zinc deposits?
technology.fact: BHP began in 1885 as the Broken Hill Proprietary Company and later became one of the world's largest mining firms.

art.q: Which Danish architect designed the Sydney Opera House?
art.fact: Utzon left the project in 1966 and never saw it completed; the building was declared a World Heritage site in 2007.

art.q: Which song begins 'Once a jolly swagman camped by a billabong'?
art.fact: The words were written in 1895 at Dagworth Station in Queensland; it is often called Australia's unofficial national anthem.

art.q: Which Sydney-formed rock band recorded 'Highway to Hell' and 'Back in Black'?
art.fact: Brothers Malcolm and Angus Young formed the band in 1973; Angus's schoolboy uniform became its trademark.

art.q: Which Australian singer had a worldwide hit with 'Can't Get You Out of My Head' in 2001?
art.fact: Kylie first became famous playing the mechanic Charlene in the TV soap 'Neighbours'.

art.q: Which 1986 film starred Paul Hogan as a bushman from the outback let loose in New York?
art.fact: It was a huge international hit, and Hogan received an Oscar nomination for co-writing the screenplay.

art.q: Which 1979 post-apocalyptic action film starring Mel Gibson launched a long-running franchise?
art.fact: Director George Miller was a medical doctor; his later 'Mad Max: Fury Road' won six Academy Awards.

art.q: Which Australian director made 'Moulin Rouge!', 'The Great Gatsby' and 'Elvis'?
art.fact: Luhrmann's 'Red Curtain' trilogy includes 'Strictly Ballroom', 'Romeo + Juliet' and 'Moulin Rouge!'.

art.q: Which wind instrument comes from Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia?
art.fact: Known to the Yolŋu people as the yidaki, it is traditionally made from a eucalyptus trunk hollowed out by termites.

art.q: Which dessert was named after the Australian opera singer Nellie Melba?
art.fact: Chef Auguste Escoffier created it in London; Melba took her stage name from her home city of Melbourne.

art.q: Which Arrernte artist became famous for his watercolour landscapes of Central Australia?
art.fact: Namatjira grew up at the Hermannsburg mission; in 1957 he became one of the first Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory granted citizenship rights.

art.q: Which painter created a famous series of works about Ned Kelly in the 1940s, showing him in his black helmet?
art.fact: Nolan painted most of the series in 1946-47; it is now held by the National Gallery of Australia in Canberra.

art.q: Which Australian author wrote the bestselling 1977 novel 'The Thorn Birds'?
art.fact: The saga of a family on a vast sheep station became a hugely popular TV mini-series in 1983.

art.q: Which Australian won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1973?
art.fact: His novel 'Voss' follows an explorer crossing the continent; he used his prize money to found an award for writers.

art.q: Which Australian novelist won the 1982 Booker Prize for 'Schindler's Ark'?
art.fact: Steven Spielberg adapted the book into the 1993 film 'Schindler's List'.

art.q: Who directed the haunting 1975 film 'Picnic at Hanging Rock'?
art.fact: Weir went on to direct Hollywood hits including 'Dead Poets Society' and 'The Truman Show'.

art.q: Which poet wrote 'My Country', with the line 'I love a sunburnt country'?
art.fact: Mackellar wrote the first version as a homesick teenager visiting England.

art.q: Which bush poet, pictured on the A$10 note, wrote 'The Man from Snowy River'?
art.fact: Andrew Barton 'Banjo' Paterson took his pen name from a racehorse his family owned.

art.q: Which American architect couple won the international competition to design Canberra in 1912?
choices: Frank Lloyd Wright and Catherine Tobin
Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin
art.fact: Marion's striking drawings helped win the competition; Canberra's central lake is named Lake Burley Griffin.

art.q: The Western Desert art movement, known for acrylic 'dot' paintings, began in 1971 at which community?
art.fact: Senior men painted a Honey Ant Dreaming mural on a school wall, inspiring the Papunya Tula artists' cooperative.

art.q: Which novel won Peter Carey his second Booker Prize, in 2001?
choices: True History of the Kelly Gang
art.fact: The novel is written as Ned Kelly's own letter to his daughter, in an unpunctuated, breathless voice.

art.q: Which Heidelberg School artist painted 'Shearing the Rams' in 1890?
art.fact: Roberts sketched in a real shearing shed for months; the painting hangs in the National Gallery of Victoria.

art.q: Which Australian architect, known for houses that 'touch the earth lightly', won the 2002 Pritzker Prize?
art.fact: Murcutt works alone and designs mainly modest homes suited to their landscape and climate.

art.q: Which Anmatyerre artist from Utopia began painting on canvas in her late seventies and created 'Earth's Creation'?
art.fact: In just eight years she produced thousands of works, and her paintings have toured major galleries around the world.

art.q: Which 1918 children's book by Norman Lindsay features a bad-tempered pudding that never runs out?
art.fact: Albert the pudding can be steak and kidney or apple dumpling, whatever his owners fancy, and regrows after every slice.

art.q: Which Australian soprano was nicknamed 'La Stupenda'?
art.fact: Italian audiences gave her the nickname after a 1960 performance in Venice; she sang at major opera houses for four decades.

politics.q: What is the capital of Australia?
politics.fact: Canberra was built as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne; Parliament moved there from Melbourne in 1927.

politics.q: Who was Australia's first prime minister?
politics.fact: A leading campaigner for Federation, Barton later became one of the first judges of the High Court of Australia.

politics.q: Who became Australia's first female prime minister in 2010?
politics.fact: Gillard was born in Barry, Wales, and moved to Adelaide with her family as a young child.

politics.q: Voting in Australian federal elections is what for adult citizens?
politics.fact: Compulsory voting began federally in 1924; turnout is usually around 90%, and elections are held on Saturdays.

politics.q: Which official represents the monarch as Australia's head of state at the national level?
politics.fact: The Governor-General is appointed by the monarch on the advice of the prime minister and lives at Government House in Canberra.

politics.q: Which prime minister was dismissed by the Governor-General on 11 November 1975?
politics.fact: Sir John Kerr dismissed Whitlam amid a budget deadlock in the Senate; it remains the most dramatic crisis in Australian politics.

politics.q: Which prime minister disappeared while swimming off a Victorian beach in December 1967?
politics.fact: His body was never found; in a famously Australian twist, a Melbourne swimming centre is named in his memory.

politics.q: In 2008, which prime minister delivered the National Apology to the Stolen Generations?
politics.fact: The apology on 13 February 2008 was the new Parliament's first business, and crowds watched on big screens across the country.

politics.q: How many states make up the Commonwealth of Australia?
politics.fact: The six states are joined by two self-governing mainland territories: the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory.

politics.q: In a 1999 referendum, Australians voted on whether to become what?
choices: A member of the Commonwealth of Nations
politics.fact: About 55% voted No to replacing the monarch with a president chosen by Parliament.

politics.q: Who is Australia's longest-serving prime minister?
politics.fact: Menzies served over 18 years in two spells, 1939-41 and 1949-66, and founded the modern Liberal Party.

politics.q: In 1894, which colony became the first in Australia to give women the vote?
politics.fact: It also became one of the first places in the world where women could stand for parliament.

politics.q: The 1967 referendum, backed by over 90% of voters, changed the Constitution so that Aboriginal people would be what?
choices: Allowed to vote for the first time
politics.fact: It also let the federal Parliament make laws for Aboriginal people; it remains the biggest Yes vote in any Australian referendum.

politics.q: The High Court's 1992 Mabo decision overturned which legal idea?
politics.fact: Eddie Mabo, from Mer in the Torres Strait, died months before the court recognised native title to his people's land.

politics.q: Which future prime minister set a record for drinking a yard of ale while studying at Oxford?
politics.fact: Hawke, a Rhodes Scholar, later said the feat may have helped his popularity with ordinary Australians.

politics.q: To change Australia's Constitution, a referendum must win a 'double majority'. What does that mean?
choices: Approval by the Senate and the High Court
Two-thirds of both houses of Parliament
Majorities in two separate votes a year apart
A national majority plus majorities in most states
politics.fact: This high bar means fewer than one in five proposals put to voters since 1901 have succeeded.

politics.q: Parliament House in Canberra opened in which year, marking 200 years since the First Fleet's arrival?
politics.fact: It is built into Capital Hill, so people can walk on grass over its roof, beneath an 81-metre flagpole.

politics.q: What is the name of the prime minister's official residence in Canberra?
politics.fact: Kirribilli House is the prime minister's Sydney residence, while Yarralumla is the Governor-General's home in Canberra.

politics.q: Who designed the Aboriginal flag, first flown in Adelaide in 1971?
politics.fact: Black represents the people, red the earth and ochre, and yellow the sun; it became an official flag of Australia in 1995.

politics.q: How many senators does each Australian state elect?
politics.fact: Every state has equal Senate representation regardless of population; the two mainland territories elect two senators each.

politics.q: In 2017-18 several federal MPs lost their seats under which section of the Constitution, which bars dual citizens?
politics.fact: The 'citizenship crisis' forced by-elections; some members had never known they held a second citizenship by descent.

politics.q: Who became the first Aboriginal member of the federal Parliament, as a senator in 1971?
politics.fact: Bonner represented Queensland in the Senate until 1983; Ken Wyatt became the first Aboriginal member of the House in 2010.

politics.q: In 1943, who became the first woman elected to the federal House of Representatives?
politics.fact: At the same election Dorothy Tangney became the first woman elected to the Senate.

politics.q: Australia's Constitution was enacted in 1900 as an Act of which parliament?
politics.fact: Queen Victoria gave royal assent to the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act on 9 July 1900.

politics.q: Which 1986 law ended the British Parliament's remaining power to legislate for Australia?
politics.fact: The Australia Act also ended appeals from Australian courts to the Privy Council in London.

current-affairs.q: What name is given to Australia's devastating 2019-20 bushfire season?
current-affairs.fact: Fires burned tens of millions of hectares, and scientists estimated that nearly 3 billion animals were killed or displaced.

current-affairs.q: Who became prime minister after Australia's May 2022 federal election?
current-affairs.fact: Albanese grew up in public housing in Sydney's inner west, raised by a single mother.

current-affairs.q: In the October 2023 referendum, Australians voted on creating what?
current-affairs.fact: The proposal did not pass: about 60% voted No nationally and it failed to win a majority in any state.

current-affairs.q: Australia co-hosted the 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup with which country?
current-affairs.fact: The Matildas reached the semi-finals for the first time, and their quarter-final penalty shoot-out win gripped the nation.

current-affairs.q: In July 2021, which Australian city was chosen to host the 2032 Summer Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: Australia's previous Summer Games were Melbourne 1956 and Sydney 2000.

current-affairs.q: From 26 October 2019, what became permanently banned at Uluru?
current-affairs.fact: The date marked 34 years since Uluru was handed back to its Anangu traditional owners, who had long asked visitors not to climb.

current-affairs.q: In January 2022, who became the first Australian in decades to win the Australian Open women's singles title?
current-affairs.fact: Barty was the first home winner of the women's title since 1978; she retired from tennis two months later, aged 25.

current-affairs.q: In October 2024, which monarch made his first visit to Australia as king?
current-affairs.fact: King Charles and Queen Camilla visited Canberra and Sydney; Charles had first come to Australia as a teenager, attending school in Victoria.

current-affairs.q: In November 2023, Australia won a record sixth men's Cricket World Cup by beating which host nation in the final?
current-affairs.fact: Travis Head scored 137 in the final in Ahmedabad, in front of a huge home crowd.

current-affairs.q: In September 2021, Australia announced the AUKUS security partnership with which two countries?
current-affairs.fact: A central part of AUKUS is helping Australia acquire nuclear-powered, conventionally armed submarines.

current-affairs.q: Which leader's party won Australia's federal election held on 3 May 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Labor was returned with an increased majority, and opposition leader Peter Dutton lost his own seat of Dickson.

current-affairs.q: In November 2024, Australia's Parliament passed a law setting what minimum age for holding social media accounts?
current-affairs.fact: The law puts the onus on platforms, not parents or children, which face heavy fines if they fail to take reasonable steps.

current-affairs.q: Which Australian swimmer, nicknamed 'the Terminator', beat Katie Ledecky to 400 m freestyle gold at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Her coach Dean Boxall's wild celebration in the stands became one of the most-shared moments of the Games.

current-affairs.q: How many gold medals did Australia win at the Paris 2024 Olympics, its best tally ever?
current-affairs.fact: Swimmers won seven of the golds, and the team finished fourth on the medal table.

current-affairs.q: In November 2021, Australia's men's cricket team won its first World Cup in which format?
current-affairs.fact: Australia beat New Zealand by eight wickets in the final in Dubai, with Mitchell Marsh named player of the match.

current-affairs.q: Who became Australia's foreign minister in May 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Born in Malaysia, Penny Wong was the first Asian-born member of an Australian federal cabinet.

current-affairs.q: Which Australian driver took his first Formula One victory at the 2024 Hungarian Grand Prix?
current-affairs.fact: Piastri, from Melbourne, won for McLaren in only his second F1 season.

current-affairs.q: In February 2021, which platform briefly blocked news for Australian users in a dispute over a new media bargaining law?
current-affairs.fact: The block lasted about a week; it ended after the government agreed to amendments and the law was passed.

current-affairs.q: How many medals did swimmer Emma McKeon win at the Tokyo Olympics, held in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Four golds and three bronzes tied the record for the most medals won by a woman at a single Olympics.

current-affairs.q: In February-March 2022, record floods devastated which northern New South Wales city?
current-affairs.fact: The Wilsons River peaked more than 2 m above its previous record, and residents in tinnies rescued neighbours from rooftops.

current-affairs.q: Who was sworn in as Australia's Governor-General on 1 July 2024?
current-affairs.fact: A businesswoman and former AFL commissioner, she became the second woman to hold the post, after Quentin Bryce.

current-affairs.q: Who became the first woman to serve as governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, in September 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Bullock joined the central bank as a graduate in 1985 and worked her way up to lead it.

current-affairs.q: In May 2020, mining company Rio Tinto destroyed ancient Aboriginal rock shelters at which site in the Pilbara?
current-affairs.fact: The shelters held evidence of human occupation going back about 46,000 years; the outcry led to the chief executive's resignation.

current-affairs.q: Under AUKUS plans announced in March 2023, Australia is to buy which class of US nuclear-powered submarine?
current-affairs.fact: The plan also includes a new jointly developed submarine, SSN-AUKUS, to be built in Britain and Australia.

current-affairs.q: Ash Barty's Wimbledon title in July 2021 came 50 years after the first Wimbledon win of which fellow Indigenous Australian?
current-affairs.fact: Barty, a Ngarigo woman, wore a dress inspired by the scalloped outfit Goolagong wore in her 1971 win.

society.q: Australia's annual inflation rate peaked in the December 2022 quarter at roughly what level?
society.fact: It was the highest annual CPI reading since 1990, driven by housing, food and fuel costs, and fell back below 3% by late 2024.

society.q: After 13 consecutive rises from May 2022, at what level did the Reserve Bank of Australia's cash rate peak in November 2023?
society.fact: The cash rate had sat at a record low of 0.10% during the pandemic; the first cut of the cycle did not come until February 2025.

society.q: Australia's 2020 JobKeeper wage subsidy initially paid eligible workers how much per fortnight?
society.fact: JobKeeper supported around 3.8 million workers at its peak and cost about $89 billion, making it the largest single programme in Australia's history.

society.q: In 2024, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported that the country's population had passed which milestone?
society.fact: Growth was driven mostly by overseas migration rather than births; the population had only passed 25 million in 2018.

society.q: In which year did Australia's revised 'stage 3' income tax cuts, which gave a cut to every taxpayer, take effect?
society.fact: The government redesigned the cuts in January 2024 to give more to lower and middle earners, and they started on 1 July that year.

society.q: In 2024, Australian employees gained a new legal right to do what outside working hours?
society.fact: The 'right to disconnect' lets staff refuse to monitor or respond to unreasonable out-of-hours contact; it applied to larger employers from August 2024.

society.q: On 1 July 2025, the compulsory superannuation guarantee paid by Australian employers reached what rate?
society.fact: The rate rose by half a percentage point each year from 9.5% in 2020-21, completing a timetable set out more than a decade earlier.

society.q: On 1 July 2023, Australia's qualifying age for the Age Pension reached what, completing a gradual rise that began in 2017?
society.fact: The age rose in six-month steps from 65; a proposal to lift it further to 70 was dropped in 2018.

society.q: The May 2024 federal budget gave every Australian household a rebate on energy bills worth how much?
society.fact: The $300 was credited in quarterly instalments over 2024-25; small businesses received $325, and the relief was later extended into 2025.

society.q: In March 2022, in response to soaring petrol prices, the federal government did what to the fuel excise for six months?
society.fact: The excise fell by 22.1 cents a litre to 22.1 cents; the cut ended as planned at the end of September 2022.

society.q: Australia's net overseas migration hit a record in 2022-23 of roughly how many people?
society.fact: The surge reflected the return of international students and workers after border closures, and migration became a major political issue.

society.q: From January 2023, the maximum general co-payment for a medicine on Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme was cut from $42.50 to what?
society.fact: It was the first cut to the PBS co-payment in the scheme's 75-year history; a further reduction to $25 was legislated for 2026.

society.q: From August 2024, Queensland introduced a flat fare on all public transport in Brisbane and across the state of how much?
society.fact: The six-month trial was made permanent in December 2024 after patronage jumped; each trip costs 50 cents regardless of distance.

society.q: In June 2023, Australian HECS-HELP student loans were indexed by what rate, the highest in over 30 years?
society.fact: The backlash led the government in 2024 to cap indexation at the lower of CPI or wage growth, and in 2025 to legislate a 20% cut to all student debts.

society.q: From 1 July 2024, Australia's national minimum wage was set at what hourly rate after a 3.75% increase?
society.fact: The Fair Work Commission sets the rate each year; it had raised it by 5.75% in 2023 and lifted it again to $24.95 in July 2025.

society.q: In mid-2022, Australia's unemployment rate fell to roughly what level, its lowest in almost 50 years?
society.fact: The rate dipped to 3.4% in October 2022, the lowest since 1974, as the labour market tightened sharply after the pandemic.

society.q: From July 2023, Australia's 'Cheaper Child Care' reforms lifted the maximum childcare subsidy for lower-income families to what share of fees?
society.fact: The changes raised the subsidy for about 1.2 million families and lifted the income cut-off to $530,000.

society.q: The 2022-23 federal budget outcome was Australia's first surplus since which financial year?
society.fact: The $22 billion surplus was helped by high commodity prices and strong employment; a second surplus followed in 2023-24.

society.q: In the 2021 Census, roughly what proportion of Australians reported having 'no religion'?
society.fact: 'No religion' was the fastest-growing response, up from 30% in 2016, while Christianity fell below half the population for the first time.

society.q: The 'Robodebt' scheme, examined by a royal commission that reported in July 2023, used automated income averaging to raise what?
society.fact: The scheme ran from 2015 to 2019 and was found unlawful; a 2020 class-action settlement was worth about $1.8 billion.

society.q: In July 2024, Australia more than doubled its international student visa application fee to what amount?
society.fact: The fee rose from $710 and was lifted again to $2,000 in July 2025, making it the most expensive student visa among major study destinations.

society.q: The May 2023 federal budget raised the maximum rate of Commonwealth Rent Assistance by what percentage, the largest rise in 30 years?
society.fact: A further 10% increase followed in the 2024 budget as rents rose sharply and vacancy rates in major cities sat near 1%.

society.q: Australia's National Housing Accord set a target of building how many new homes in the five years from July 2024?
society.fact: The target was lifted from an initial 1 million in 2023; it equates to 240,000 homes a year, well above recent building rates.

society.q: From February 2024, Australia's Workplace Gender Equality Agency began publishing gender pay gaps for employers with at least how many employees?
society.fact: Around 5,000 employers were named in the first release, which showed a median total pay gap of about 19% in favour of men.

society.q: In November 2023, the federal government changed the Medicare bulk-billing incentive for GP visits by children and concession card holders in what way?
society.fact: The $3.5 billion measure aimed to reverse a slide in bulk billing; in 2025 the incentive was extended to all patients.

general.q: What is the Aboriginal name of the giant sandstone rock in Central Australia once called Ayers Rock?
general.fact: Uluru is sacred to the Anangu people, who jointly manage Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park; it glows red at sunset.

general.q: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the coast of which Australian state?
general.fact: Stretching about 2,300 km, it is the world's largest coral reef system and was World Heritage-listed in 1981.

general.q: Which egg-laying Australian mammal has a duck-like bill and webbed feet?
general.fact: Male platypuses have venomous spurs on their hind legs, and the bill senses the electric fields of prey underwater.

general.q: Which Sydney beach is famous for its surf lifesavers and the Icebergs ocean pool?
general.fact: Bondi's surf lifesaving club, founded in 1907, is one of the oldest in the world.

general.q: Which dark, salty spread made from leftover brewer's yeast was created in Melbourne in 1922?
general.fact: Food scientist Cyril Callister developed it; Australians are told to spread it thinly on buttered toast.

general.q: Which cricketer finished his Test career with a batting average of 99.94?
general.fact: Bradman needed just four runs in his final innings to average 100, but he was bowled for a duck.

general.q: The limestone sea stacks called the Twelve Apostles stand beside which famous coastal road?
general.fact: There were never twelve stacks. The road itself was built by returned First World War soldiers as a war memorial.

general.q: Which horse race is known as 'the race that stops a nation'?
general.fact: Run on the first Tuesday of November, it is a public holiday in Melbourne; the famous racehorse Phar Lap won it in 1930.

general.q: In Australian slang, what is an 'arvo'?
general.fact: Australians love shortening words: a 'servo' is a petrol station and a 'brekkie' is breakfast.

general.q: What is Australia's national floral emblem?
general.fact: Its green and gold colours inspired Australia's national sporting colours, and 1 September is National Wattle Day.

general.q: Which island off Queensland, the world's largest sand island, was officially renamed K'gari in 2023?
general.fact: K'gari is the Butchulla people's name for the island, which has rainforest growing on sand and dozens of freshwater lakes.

general.q: What is mainland Australia's highest mountain?
general.fact: At 2,228 m, it was named by Polish explorer Paweł Strzelecki after the Polish-Lithuanian hero Tadeusz Kościuszko.

general.q: Kakadu National Park, famous for wetlands and ancient rock art, is in which state or territory?
general.fact: Kakadu is jointly managed with its Bininj/Mungguy traditional owners, and its rock art spans thousands of years.

general.q: What is Australia's longest river?
general.fact: The Murray flows about 2,500 km from the Australian Alps to the sea in South Australia, forming much of the NSW-Victoria border.

general.q: The last known thylacine, or 'Tasmanian tiger', died in a Hobart zoo in which year?
general.fact: The striped marsupial carnivore died on 7 September 1936; that date is now Australia's National Threatened Species Day.

general.q: Which outback opal-mining town is famous for homes and churches built underground?
general.fact: Underground 'dugouts' stay comfortably cool while summer temperatures outside can top 45°C.

general.q: Kata Tjuta, the group of huge domed rocks near Uluru, was formerly known by what name?
general.fact: Kata Tjuta means 'many heads'; its tallest dome, Mount Olga, rises higher than Uluru.

general.q: Which square sponge cake dipped in chocolate and coated in coconut is an Australian classic?
general.fact: It is named after Lord Lamington, governor of Queensland from 1896 to 1901.

general.q: Which AFL club, founded in 1858, is one of the oldest football clubs of any code in the world?
general.fact: Australian rules football was codified in Melbourne in 1859, partly to keep cricketers fit during the winter.

general.q: Roughly how long is the Dingo Fence, built to keep dingoes out of sheep country in south-eastern Australia?
general.fact: It is one of the longest fences in the world, stretching from Queensland's Darling Downs to South Australia's Great Australian Bight.

general.q: Lake Hillier, famous for its bubble-gum pink water, lies on an island off which state?
general.fact: The lake on Middle Island in the Recherche Archipelago gets its colour from salt-loving algae and microbes.

general.q: The English word 'kangaroo' comes from 'gangurru' in which Aboriginal language?
general.fact: Joseph Banks and James Cook recorded the word in 1770 while repairing the Endeavour at today's Cooktown.

general.q: The beehive-striped domes of the Bungle Bungle Range are protected in which Western Australian national park?
general.fact: Although long known to local Aboriginal people, the range was little known to other Australians until the 1980s.

general.q: What is Australia's lowest natural point, about 15 m below sea level?
general.fact: Usually a dry salt crust, the lake fills completely only a few times a century, when it attracts huge flocks of pelicans.

general.q: Which outback town holds the Henley-on-Todd Regatta, with bottomless boats 'raced' along a dry riverbed?
general.fact: Crews poke their legs through their boats and run along the sandy bed of the Todd River, which is usually dry.
